title: Rust & Systems Programming
summary: Ownership, borrowing and the type system, checked by the real compiler.

objectives.title: A non-Copy value moves on assignment
Copy types are duplicated, not moved
Shared references read without taking ownership
Only one mutable reference at a time

body.text: Every value in Rust has exactly one owner. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped.
A String keeps its text on the heap. Writing `let b = a;` doesn't copy that text. It hands ownership from `a` to `b`, and `a` can't be used afterwards.
Make a prediction before you check each answer. A wrong guess teaches you more than a lucky one.

steps.title: What happens when this runs?

body.text: Read the program and predict what the compiler and the program do.

options.text: It doesn't compile: `route` was moved into `saved`.
It compiles, then panics at run time.

misconceptions.a: Assigning a String doesn't copy its heap text. Ownership moves to `saved`, so the compiler rejects the later use of `route`.
misconceptions.b: Nothing runs. Rust finds the use of a moved value at compile time.
misconceptions.d: Rust doesn't wait for run time here. The borrow checker rejects the program before it's built.

hints: Think about how many owners the text "north ridge" can have at once.
After `let saved = route;`, which variable owns the String?
Using a variable after its value has moved is a compile-time error (E0382).

correct.text: Right. `saved` now owns the String, so `route` is no longer usable. rustc reports E0382: borrow of moved value.

steps.title: Which of these types are Copy?

body.text: A Copy type is duplicated bit for bit on assignment, so the original stays usable. Select every type that is Copy.

misconceptions.string: A String owns heap memory. Copying it bit for bit would give two owners of the same buffer, so it moves instead.
misconceptions.vec: A Vec owns a heap buffer, so like a String it moves on assignment.

hints: Ask whether the type owns memory on the heap.
A tuple is Copy when every field in it is Copy.
Shared references such as `&str` are Copy. Copying a reference doesn't copy what it points to.

correct.text: Right. Scalars, tuples of Copy fields and shared references are Copy. String and Vec own heap buffers, so they move.

solution.text: Copy: i32, bool, (u8, char), &str. Not Copy: String, Vec<u8>.

steps.title: Keep both names usable

body.text: Fill in the method so that `route` and `saved` both own their own String, and `route` can still be printed.

hints: You need a second, independent String.
The method makes a deep copy of the heap text.
It's the method from the `Clone` trait.

correct.text: Right. `clone()` allocates a new String, so each variable has its own owner. Clones are explicit because they cost an allocation.

body.text: This has the same shape as the first program, but the type is different. Predict the result.

misconceptions.b: u32 is Copy. Assignment duplicates the value, so `depth` stays usable.

steps.title: Transfer: passing a String to a function

body.text: Calling a function with a value works like assigning it to the parameter. Predict the result.

options.text: It doesn't compile: `shout` returns the wrong type.

misconceptions.a: `shout` takes a String by value, so it takes ownership. `name` can't be used after the call.
misconceptions.c: `text.len()` returns usize, which matches the signature. The problem is the later use of `name`.

hints: What does the parameter type `String` (not `&String`) mean for the caller?
Ownership of `name` moves into `text` at the call.

correct.text: Right. A by-value parameter takes ownership. Borrowing is the next lesson's fix.

body.text: A reference lets code use a value without owning it. `&T` is a shared reference, and you may hold as many of them as you like.
`&mut T` is a mutable reference. While one is in use, no other reference to the same value may be used, shared or mutable.
A reference is in use from where it's created to where it's last used, not to the end of the block.

steps.title: Lend the String to a function

body.text: This time the function takes `&String`. Predict the result.

misconceptions.b: `&line` lends a shared reference, so `main` keeps ownership of `line`.
misconceptions.c: `w` borrows from `line`, and `line` lives until the end of `main`, so the borrow is fine.

hints: Look at the `&` in the call and in the parameter type.
Several shared reads of `line` may be in use at once.

correct.text: Right. A shared borrow lets `first_word` read `line` while `main` keeps owning it.

steps.title: Which line stops this from compiling?

body.text: Exactly one line makes the compiler reject this program.

misconceptions.l3: Taking a shared reference is fine on its own. The conflict comes when something needs `&mut scores` while `first` is still in use.
misconceptions.l5: rustc reports the error where the conflicting mutable borrow happens. Line 5 is only the reason `first` is still in use.

hints: `push` needs `&mut scores`.
Is `first` still in use when `push` runs?
A push may reallocate the buffer, which would leave `first` pointing at freed memory.

correct.text: Right. Line 4 needs a mutable borrow while the shared borrow `first` is still in use on line 5 (E0502).

solution.text: error[E0502]: cannot borrow `scores` as mutable because it is also borrowed as immutable

steps.title: Order the lines so the program prints 8

body.text: These are the lines inside `fn main()`. Put them in an order that compiles and prints `8`.

hints: A variable must be declared before it's borrowed.
`println!` borrows `total` too, so the mutable reference must be finished first.

correct.text: Right. The mutable borrow `r` ends at its last use, `*r += 3;`, so `println!` can then read `total`.

steps.title: Fix it with the compiler

body.text: This program doesn't compile. Change it so that it compiles and prints `9 2`, without cloning the vector.
Your code runs only in SAIL's isolated sandbox. If the sandbox isn't available, this step is shown as not assessed.

hints: Read the compiler's first error: what type does `longest` expect?
`longest` wants a reference, but the call passes the Vec itself.
Pass `&words` so `main` keeps ownership.

steps.title: Transfer: two mutable references

body.text: Predict the result.

options.text: It doesn't compile: `log` is borrowed as mutable twice.
It compiles, but `a` and `b` race at run time.

misconceptions.b: `a` is still in use when `b` is created, so there would be two live mutable references. Rust rejects that (E0499).
misconceptions.c: Rust prevents this aliasing at compile time, so the program never runs.

hints: Is `a` still in use when `b` is created?
Only one `&mut` may be live at a time.

correct.text: Right. E0499: `a` is used after `b` is created, so two mutable borrows overlap.

solution.text: It doesn't compile (E0499). Use `a` before you create `b`.

reviews.title: Review: a struct with a String field

body.text: Predict the result.

reviews.title: Review: looping over a Vec

body.text: Predict the result.

options.text: It doesn't compile: the loop moved `names`.

misconceptions.a: `for n in names` calls `into_iter()` on the Vec itself, which consumes it. Use `&names` to loop without moving.

Compare `for n in names` with `for n in &names`.

correct.text: Right. Looping over the Vec by value moves it into the loop.

reviews.title: Review: copy or move?

body.text: Select every snippet that compiles.

options.text: let x = 7u8; let y = x; println!("{x}");
let s = String::from("7"); let t = s; println!("{s}");
let s = String::from("7"); let t = s.clone(); println!("{s}");

misconceptions.b: The String moved into `t`, so printing `s` is a use after move.

hints: Which of these values are Copy?
An explicit `clone()` leaves the original usable.

correct.text: Right. u8 copies, a moved String can't be reused, and a clone keeps both.

body.text: Predict the result.

reviews.title: Review: pushing while iterating

body.text: Predict the result.

options.text: It doesn't compile: `stack` is mutably borrowed while the loop borrows it.
It runs forever, doubling the vector.

misconceptions.b: Rust rejects this before it runs: `push` needs `&mut stack` while the loop holds `&stack`.
misconceptions.c: The loop's shared borrow is live for the whole loop, so `push` can't borrow mutably inside it.

hints: What does `for x in &stack` borrow, and for how long?

correct.text: Right. E0502: the loop's shared borrow overlaps with the mutable borrow `push` needs.
